# kchitnis

> Malware teardowns, threat intel, and detection notes. The personal blog of Kshitij Chitnis.

Technical writing on malware analysis, reverse engineering, detection engineering, and CTF challenges. This index covers every published post.

## Pages

- [About](https://kchitnis.com/about/): Security researcher interested in threat intelligence, malware teardowns, and the tools I build.
- [Resume](https://kchitnis.com/resume/): Incident response and SOC analyst with 4-5 years across security operations, threat detection, and penetration testing.
- [Art](https://kchitnis.com/art/): Drawings and visual work.
- [Music](https://kchitnis.com/music/): Music I have made.

## Posts

- [FakeGit's LuaJIT Loader: Hidden Strings and a Polygon Dead Drop](https://kchitnis.com/posts/fakegit-luajit-loader/): A GitHub repository named StanLeyJ03/mcp-for-security advertised a collection of Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers wrapping security tools like SQLMap, FFUF, NMAP, and Masscan for AI agents.
- [PaperCut's Pre-Auth RCE: What the IOCs and the Payload Tell Us](https://kchitnis.com/posts/papercut-zero-day/): On August 27, PaperCut issued an advisory warning of in-the-wild exploitation against PaperCut NG and MF servers.
- [JavaScript Obfuscation: From Party Trick to Phishing Kit](https://kchitnis.com/posts/js-obfuscation-phishing/): When triaging phishing pages and malicious scripts, understanding how JavaScript obfuscation works makes deobfuscation much faster.
- [SLEEPWALKER: The Backdoor That Does Nothing Until a Packet Says Otherwise](https://kchitnis.com/posts/sleepwalker-backdoor/): SLEEPWALKER is a 59,904-byte Windows DLL designed to run passively inside an enterprise environment.
- [405 AI Malware Samples, and Almost None of Them Ever Deployed](https://kchitnis.com/posts/ai-enabled-malware/): Unit 42 gathered 405 malware samples associated with AI, including brand impersonation kits, LLM-generated code, and agentic execution loops.
- [Weedhack: SEO Poisoning the Minecraft Client Scene](https://kchitnis.com/posts/weedhack-seo-minecraft/): A campaign documented by McAfee shows how attackers use search engine optimization (SEO) poisoning to outrank legitimate open-source utility websites across Google, Bing, Brave, and DuckDuckGo.
- [WordlistLoader: Shellcode Hidden as Plain English Words](https://kchitnis.com/posts/wordlistloader-amatera/): WordlistLoader is an obfuscated loader that encodes shellcode as a dictionary of ordinary English words.
- [RedC2: A $99 C2 Framework Shipping Through npm](https://kchitnis.com/posts/redc2-npm/): Trend Micro identified 14 trojanized npm packages delivering a Linux implant for RedC2 4.0, a commercial command-and-control framework sold openly on the web for $99.99 under the name Red Offsec.
- [N4D: The MCP Exploitation Framework That Scans Like a Botnet](https://kchitnis.com/posts/n4d-mcp-exploitation/): N4D was first documented in June as an exploitation tool targeting Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.
- [SPECTRE: The Cross-Platform Implant With a Rootkit and a Driver](https://kchitnis.com/posts/spectre-implant/): Cisco Talos published an analysis of the UAT-10147 toolkit, centered on SPECTRE, a cross-platform backdoor written in C.
- [AmnesiaStealer: The macOS Malware That Double-Checks Your Password Before Stealing It](https://kchitnis.com/posts/amnesia-stealer/): AmnesiaStealer is a Rust-based macOS stealer that verifies entered passwords before attempting to use them.
- [Mythos 5 Tried to Backdoor a Real Open Source Project](https://kchitnis.com/posts/mythos-backdoor-attempt/): In an August 2026 report, the UK AI Safety Institute (AISI) documented an incident where an autonomous agent running Claude Mythos 5 spent 34 hours attempting to merge a backdoor into a real open-source repository.
- [NullReceiver: Hiding a C2 IP in a Fake Ethereum Address](https://kchitnis.com/posts/nullreceiver-ethereum-c2/): Earlier blockchain C2 techniques, commonly grouped under EtherHiding, stored payload strings inside smart contracts on public ledgers.
- [Clicking 'Trust This Folder' Is Running Code](https://kchitnis.com/posts/coding-agent-project-trust/): When a developer clones an unfamiliar repository and clicks "trust this folder" in an AI coding assistant, code can execute immediately, before entering any prompt or approving any command.
- [Tenda, Temu, and the Root Password Printed on the Serial Console](https://kchitnis.com/posts/router-teardowns/): A recent security review of the Tenda AC10 V6 highlights common hardware security oversights in consumer routers: an unauthenticated endpoint enables a Telnet daemon, and the dynamically generated root password is printed directly to the serial console during factory resets.
- [Tengu Botnet: The Malware Reboots Your Box When You Kill It](https://kchitnis.com/posts/tengu-botnet-watchdog/): Nozomi Networks published an analysis of Tengu, an IoT botnet with an aggressive self-defense mechanism: terminating the main malware process triggers an immediate device reboot, allowing its persistence scripts to restart the payload automatically.
- [How eBPF Rootkits Manipulate System Inspection Tools](https://kchitnis.com/posts/ebpf-rootkit-detection/): eBPF rootkits generally evade detection by modifying the data that user-space auditing tools retrieve from the kernel.
- [The Newtonsoft.Json Fork That Rigged a Betting Platform](https://kchitnis.com/posts/newtonsoft-rigging/): A typosquatted package on NuGet demonstrates how targeted supply-chain malware can operate: rather than harvesting generic credentials or deploying standard backdoors, it behaved as a fully functional JSON serializer while manipulating the outcome of a specific online betting game.
- [Rogue Agents: What ProjectDiscovery Saw When Models Escaped Their Sandboxes](https://kchitnis.com/posts/rogue-agents-evals/): ProjectDiscovery published findings from their internal benchmark evaluations, detailing how autonomous models behave when they encounter dead ends during security challenges.
- [copy.fail: Four Bytes of Scratch Data and You're Root](https://kchitnis.com/posts/linux-broke/): A compact 732-byte Python script surfaced recently that achieves reliable root privilege escalation across almost every mainstream Linux distribution released since 2017.
- [From Pentester to SOC: Why Detection Engineers Need Red Team Experience](https://kchitnis.com/posts/pentester-to-soc/): I spent years breaking into systems before I started defending them.
- [VEIL#DROP: The Malware That Builds a New URL for Every Victim](https://kchitnis.com/posts/veildrop-dynamic-urls/): Securonix published an analysis of VEIL#DROP, a multi-stage loader delivering the PureLogs infostealer.
- [The SIEM That Lets You In: Splunk's Pre-Auth RCE](https://kchitnis.com/posts/splunk-sidecar-rce/): When security researchers published an analysis of CVE-2026-20253, a pre-authentication RCE in Splunk Enterprise, it caught my attention immediately as someone who works with Splunk every day.
- [The ActiveMQ RCE That Sat in Plain Sight for 13 Years](https://kchitnis.com/posts/activemq-jolokia-rce/): CVE-2026-34197 is a remote code execution vulnerability in Apache ActiveMQ Classic that went unnoticed for 13 years.
- [The npm Worm That Used GitHub as Its C2](https://kchitnis.com/posts/npm-worm-github-c2/): The shhallucinate npm worm stands out mainly for its C2 design: it ran its command channel directly through GitHub Actions discussions.
- [MSG_OOB: The Esoteric Kernel Feature That Became a Sandbox Escape](https://kchitnis.com/posts/msgoob-sandbox-escape/): In August 2025, Project Zero published a writeup detailing CVE-2025-38236, a use-after-free in Linux's MSG_OOB support for UNIX domain sockets.
- [Cookies Writeup (PicoCTF)](https://kchitnis.com/posts/cookies-picoctf/): Looking at the website provided, if we try and enter an arbitrary input, it would prompt us that the input is invalid.
- [deadcode Writeup (DownUnder CTF 2021)](https://kchitnis.com/posts/deadcode/): The binary compares the variable _var_8h with deadc0de and if true, runs a shell.
- [Filestore Writeup (Google CTF 2021)](https://kchitnis.com/posts/filestore-writeup/): We stored our flag on this platform, but forgot to save the id. Can you help us restore it?
- [Formatting Writeup (ImaginaryCTF 2021)](https://kchitnis.com/posts/formatting/): The challenge is a python file. If we run the service using the netcat utility and give some random input, it returns the same string.
- [Like a sieve Writeup (DownUnder CTF 2021)](https://kchitnis.com/posts/like-a-sieve/): From the decompiled code we can see that the last printf call does not have a format specifier.
- [no strings Writeup (DownUnder CTF 2021)](https://kchitnis.com/posts/no-strings/): The code doesn't seem to give out the flag in anyway.
- [outBackdoor Writeup (DownUnder CTF 2021)](https://kchitnis.com/posts/outbackdoor/): There is a sym.outBackdoor function in the binary at 0x004011d7
- [Roos world Writeup (ImaginaryCTF 2021)](https://kchitnis.com/posts/roos-world/): The source code of the webpage had a comment written in JSFuck.
- [Saas Writeup (ImaginaryCTF 2021)](https://kchitnis.com/posts/saas/): The challenge is to bypass the checks to get the flag. The description gave the basic idea that it uses sed.
